description:
Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

metric_notes.cost: 100 x the opponents' share of all points in the instance's games (the instance's cost)
metric_notes.win_pct: % of the instance's games in which the policy scored more points than its opponent
metric_notes.worst_share: the opponents' share of points (%) against the opponent that did best against the policy
metric_notes.flips_per_claim: opponent cells flipped per claim the policy made
metric_notes.lost_per_game: policy cells flipped to the opponent per game
metric_notes.claim_value: mean points of the cells the policy claimed (not counting flips)

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `moves`: shape (k,), int: the cells you may claim (the candidates), in random order. Index into the per-cell arrays below.
- `owner`: shape (N,), int8: for every cell on the board: 1 = yours, -1 = the opponent's, 0 = empty (N = number of cells).
- `homes`: shape (2,), int: your home cell and the opponent's home cell (homes never flip).
- `points`: shape (N,), int: what each cell is worth (1, 2 or 5).
- `adjacency`: shape (N, N), bool: which cells are neighbours (symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `turn`: int: how many claims (by both players) have been made so far in this game; the game lasts N - 2 claims.
- Your current score is `points[owner == 1].sum()`, the opponent's `points[owner == -1].sum()`.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)). The highest-scoring candidate is claimed.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

Approaches — kinds of measurements for a territory game with claiming and flipping:

1. **Immediate points value of the claimed cell** — grab high-value cells (5-point cells) early. Simple.

2. **Flip gain / flip potential**: simulate or approximate the flip outcome of claiming each candidate: how much opponent value would flip to me, and how much of my value is at risk. Compute my neighbours count vs opponent neighbours count around each opponent cell adjacent to the candidate.

3. **Frontier / adjacency exposure**: prefer cells where I have many owned neighbours and opponent has few — consolidation, defensibility. Claim cells with high own-neighbour count (protected interior) vs cells adjacent to opponent.

4. **Denial / blocking opponent's best claim**: measure how much the candidate would help the opponent (if opponent claimed it) — deny high-value cells the opponent could reach, especially 5-point cells near their frontier.

5. **Connectivity / expansion potential**: number of empty neighbours of the candidate (how much future expansion it opens), plus graph centrality (distance to remaining empty region).

6. **Tempo / claiming order pressure**: value of claiming now vs opponent's threat — measure the opponent's flip pressure on candidate cells adjacent to owned cells; defensive priority for cells of mine at risk of flipping.

7. **Score-difference win-condition awareness**: maximize (my points + potential) - opponent; weight points by scarcity, aggressive when behind.

8. **Home safety / home-adjacency**: distance from opponent home; proximity to opponent home to attack.

9. **Flip risk of my own cells after claiming** — measure opponent's ability to flip back.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
```
```python
    """Net point swing of the immediate claim+flip: points gained by me minus points the opponent loses, per candidate, normalised."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    # neighbours counts for each cell
    # For each candidate c: after claiming c, my ownership gains 1 at c.
    # A neighbour v of c owned by opponent flips if my_neighbours(v) >= opp_neighbours(v) after claim,
    # and v is not opponent's home.
    adj = adjacency.astype(np.int32)
    my_count = adj @ my.astype(np.int32)      # (N,) my neighbours per cell
    opp_count = adj @ opp.astype(np.int32)    # (N,) opp neighbours per cell
    # after claiming candidate c, my_count at neighbour v increases by 1 if adj[v,c]
    cand = moves
    # my_count_after[v, c] = my_count[v] + adj[v,c]
    # flip condition at v given candidate c: v opponent, v != opp home, and my_count[v]+adj[v,c] >= opp_count[v]
    opp_home = homes[1]
    is_opp_cell = opp & (np.arange(N) != opp_home)
    # build (N, k)
    adj_c = adj[:, cand].astype(np.int32)             # (N, k)
    my_after = my_count[:, None] + adj_c              # (N, k)

    total_pts = float(points.sum()) + 1e-9
    return (claim_pts + flip_pts) / total_pts
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
```
```python
    """Flip potential: own-neighbour count minus opponent-neighbour count around each candidate, plus the points of nearby enemy cells that would become flippable."""
    moves = np.asarray(moves, dtype=int)
    own = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    N = owner.shape[0]
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)

    # neighbours of each candidate
    nb = adj[moves]  # (k, N)

    # counts of my / opponent's neighbours for each candidate
    my_nb = nb @ own
    opp_nb = nb @ opp

    # after claiming the candidate, I gain one adjacent influence; flip condition per enemy neighbour:
    # enemy cell flips if, after my claim, my neighbour count >= its owner's count.
    # Approximate: for each candidate, sum over enemy neighbours of (-1 if they'd flip else +1) * points
    # enemy cell e flips vs candidate c if adj[c,e] and my_nb_of_e (incl. c) >= opp_nb_of_e
    # my_nb_of_e excludes c currently since c is empty; after claim c is mine so +adj[c,e]
    # Compute per enemy cell e: my_nbr_count = own @ adj[e]  (I own cells adjacent to e)
    my_adj_e = adj @ own    # (N,) number of my cells adjacent to each cell
    opp_adj_e = adj @ opp   # (N,) number of opponent cells adjacent to each cell

    # For candidate c adjacent to enemy e: after claiming c, my count at e becomes my_adj_e[e]+1
    # flips if my_adj_e[e]+1 >= opp_adj_e[e]
    # Only for enemy neighbours e of c.
    flips = (my_adj_e[None, :] + 1.0 >= opp_adj_e[None, :])  # (N, N) true where e would flip if c adjacent

    # lost potential: enemy neighbours that DON'T flip
    noflip = nb * (~flips) * enemy_ind[None, :]
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
```
    """Flip potential: own-neighbour count minus opponent-neighbour count around each candidate, plus the points of nearby enemy cells that would become flippable."""
    moves = np.asarray(moves, dtype=int)
    own = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    N = owner.shape[0]
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)

    # neighbours of each candidate
    nb = adj[moves]  # (k, N)

    # counts of my / opponent's neighbours for each candidate
    my_nb = nb @ own
    opp_nb = nb @ opp

    # after claiming the candidate, I gain one adjacent influence; flip condition per enemy neighbour:
    # enemy cell flips if, after my claim, my neighbour count >= its owner's count.
    # Approximate: for each candidate, sum over enemy neighbours of (-1 if they'd flip else +1) * points
    # enemy cell e flips vs candidate c if adj[c,e] and my_nb_of_e (incl. c) >= opp_nb_of_e
    # my_nb_of_e excludes c currently since c is empty; after claim c is mine so +adj[c,e]
    # Compute per enemy cell e: my_nbr_count = own @ adj[e]  (I own cells adjacent to e)
    my_adj_e = adj @ own    # (N,) number of my cells adjacent to each cell
    opp_adj_e = adj @ opp   # (N,) number of opponent cells adjacent to each cell

    # For candidate c adjacent to enemy e: after claiming c, my count at e becomes my_adj_e[e]+1
    # flips if my_adj_e[e]+1 >= opp_adj_e[e]
    # Only for enemy neighbours e of c.
    flips = (my_adj_e[None, :] + 1.0 >= opp_adj_e[None, :])  # (N, N) true where e would flip if c adjacent
    # weight by enemy + adjacency + points
    enemy_ind = opp  # (N,)
    flip_gain = nb * flips * enemy_ind[None, :] * points[None, :]  # (k, N)
    flip_pts = flip_gain.sum(axis=1)  # points flipped

    # lost potential: enemy neighbours that DON'T flip
    noflip = nb * (~flips) * enemy_ind[None, :]
    noflip_cnt = noflip.sum(axis=1)

    # value of cell itself
    cand_pts = points[moves].astype(float)

    # combine: prefer flipping high-value cells, and cells with more own neighbours than opp
    score = (flip_pts / 10.0) - 0.3 * noflip_cnt + 0.2 * (my_nb - opp_nb) + 0.1 * cand_pts
    # normalise
    scale = np.abs(score).max()
    if scale > 1e-9:
        score = score / scale
    return score

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Points of opponent cells that would flip immediately after claiming each candidate, weighted by how close the flip is to failing (margin of the neighbour count), normalised by total board points."""
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    theirs = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    my_nb = adjacency @ mine
    op_nb = adjacency @ theirs
    adj_m = adjacency[moves]                      # (k, N)
    opp_cell = (owner == -1)[None, :]             # (1, N)
    allow = np.ones(owner.shape[0], bool)
    allow[homes[1]] = False
    my_after = my_nb[None, :] + adj_m             # (k, N)
    margin = my_after - op_nb[None, :]            # >=0 means flip
    flips = opp_cell & adj_m & allow[None, :] & (margin >= 0)
    # smooth weight: 1 at margin 0 (barely flips), decaying as margin grows (robust flip)
    weight = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.maximum(margin, 0.0))
    gain = (flips * weight * points[None, :]).sum(axis=1)
    return gain / max(points.sum(), 1.0)

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `moves`: shape (k,), int: the cells you may claim (the candidates), in random order. Index into the per-cell arrays below.
- `owner`: shape (N,), int8: for every cell on the board: 1 = yours, -1 = the opponent's, 0 = empty (N = number of cells).
- `homes`: shape (2,), int: your home cell and the opponent's home cell (homes never flip).
- `points`: shape (N,), int: what each cell is worth (1, 2 or 5).
- `adjacency`: shape (N, N), bool: which cells are neighbours (symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `turn`: int: how many claims (by both players) have been made so far in this game; the game lasts N - 2 claims.
- Your current score is `points[owner == 1].sum()`, the opponent's `points[owner == -1].sum()`.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)). The highest-scoring candidate is claimed.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

You are the **Researcher** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You are the deep loop: you work out *why* the current best candidate loses where it does, and you design experiments that find out. The Mutator, another agent, makes undirected variations; you cash in on what it stumbles on and on what your own experiments reveal.

## What you get

- the incumbent (the current best) and its parts: what each part actually does and how much the result relies on it;
- **diagnostics**: named metrics of the incumbent's results, next to a reference where one exists. This is where the mechanism shows;
- **sensitivity probes**: each part of the incumbent knocked out, weakened and amplified. A gain from amplifying means a direction is under-used; a loss from weakening means the incumbent relies on it;
- the **ledger** for the approaches you're assigned: what was tried, how it scored, and whether its prediction held;
- the **Mutator's recent finds**: things that scored well or nearly well without anyone knowing why. Explaining and sharpening a lucky find is often the best experiment available;
- your **assignments** from the Navigator: which approaches to work on, and how (explore a new one, exploit a promising one, probe a doubtful one).

## How to work

1. **Find a mechanism, not a symptom.** Name a concrete difference between the incumbent's results and the reference (or between what works and what doesn't), and the decision that produces it.
2. **Design experiments of two kinds:**
   - `probe`: written to *learn*. Change one thing, or exaggerate one aspect, so the result tells you whether that aspect matters. Judged by whether its prediction held, not by its score.
   - `improve`: written to *win*.
3. **Don't repeat the ledger.** If an idea was tried, change it meaningfully or leave it. A disguised copy is detected and discarded. When the ledger shows a group of tried features that behave alike, that idea is spent: look at a different quantity altogether.
4. **Learn from what failed.** A prediction that didn't hold means the mechanism you believed is wrong or incomplete. Say what it taught you (`lesson`) before proposing the next experiment.
5. **Predict.** Every experiment names one metric from the diagnostics, where it should move (a family or scope), and the direction. The engine checks it.
6. **Be exact** in `change`: describe the candidate so precisely that it can be written without guessing.

The incumbent is a policy: a weighted sum of **features** (measurements of a candidate in one decision). An optimiser fits the weights and their signs, so never choose numbers or signs: choose *what to measure*. # The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

experiments.hypothesis: f001, f003 and f006 are one idea (|rho|>=0.9) because they all weight a flip by how close it is to succeeding. That is a re-expression, not a new measurement.
```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Immediate claim+flip point gain minus the opponent's best immediate claim+flip reply, normalised by total points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    k = moves.shape[0]
    N = owner.shape[0]

    A = adj[moves]                                   # (k,N)
    my_nb = adj @ (owner == 1).astype(float)         # (N,)
    opp_nb = adj @ (owner == -1).astype(float)       # (N,)

    opp_nonhome = (owner == -1).copy()
    opp_nonhome[homes[1]] = False

    flips = (A > 0) & opp_nonhome[None, :] & (my_nb[None, :] + A >= opp_nb[None, :])  # (k,N)
    my_gain = pts[moves] + flips.astype(float) @ pts  # (k,)

    # Post-claim boards
    new_my = np.tile((owner == 1)[None, :], (k, 1))
    new_my[np.arange(k), moves] = True
    new_my |= flips
    new_opp = np.tile((owner == -1)[None, :], (k, 1)) & ~flips

    my_cnt = new_my.astype(float) @ adj               # (k,N)
    opp_cnt = new_opp.astype(float) @ adj             # (k,N)

    # Opponent legal replies: empty cells adjacent to opponent cells, excluding the just-claimed cell
    legal = ((new_opp.astype(float) @ adj) > 0) & (owner == 0)[None, :]
    legal[np.arange(k), moves] = False

    my_nonhome = (owner == 1).copy()
    my_nonhome[homes[0]] = False

    # cond[i,e,d]: opponent claiming e flips my cell d
    cond = (opp_cnt[:, None, :] + adj[None, :, :] >= my_cnt[:, None, :]) & my_nonhome[None, None, :]
    reply = pts[None, :] + np.einsum('ied,d->ie', cond.astype(float), pts)  # (k,N)
    reply = np.where(legal, reply, 0.0)
    best_reply = reply.max(axis=1)                    # (k,)

    return (my_gain - best_reply) / tot
```

This computes, per candidate, my immediate claim+flip point gain minus the opponent's best immediate claim+flip reply value (max over legal empty replies, 0 if none), divided by total board points; I read "best reply" as the opponent's maximum reply value and treat the just-claimed cell as unavailable to the opponent.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Points of empty cells I reach strictly sooner than the opponent after claiming each candidate, normalised by total points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    INF = 1e6
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    emp = (owner == 0)

    def bfs(sources, allowed):
        d = np.full(N, INF, dtype=float)
        d[sources] = 0.0
        for step in range(1, N + 1):
            frontier = (d == step - 1)
            if not frontier.any():
                break
            nb = frontier.astype(float) @ adj
            new = (nb > 0) & (d > step) & allowed
            if not new.any():
                break
            d[new] = step
        return d

    d_me = bfs(my, emp | my)
    d_op = bfs(opp, emp | opp)

    k = moves.shape[0]
    d_m = np.full((k, N), INF, dtype=float)
    d_m[np.arange(k), moves] = 0.0
    for step in range(1, N + 1):
        frontier = (d_m == step - 1)
        if not frontier.any():
            break
        nb = frontier.astype(float) @ adj
        new = (nb > 0) & (d_m > step) & emp[None, :]
        if not new.any():
            break
        d_m[new] = step

    d_new = np.minimum(d_me[None, :], d_m)
    margin = d_op[None, :] - d_new
    weight = (margin > 0).astype(float) + 0.5 * (margin == 0).astype(float)
    val = pts[None, :] * weight * emp[None, :]
    return val.sum(axis=1) / tot
```

This computes, for each candidate, the total points of empty cells that I would reach strictly sooner than the opponent (half credit for ties) after claiming it, using BFS distances through claimable cells, normalised by total board points; I read "reach" as graph distance through empty-or-own cells for me and empty-or-opponent cells for the opponent, and treat the candidate itself as my distance-0 source.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Points of empty cells adjacent to opponent non-home cells this claim would flip, weighted by how contested each flipped cell is (own vs opponent neighbour balance), normalised by total board points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    A = adj[moves]                                   # (k, N)
    my_nb = adj @ (owner == 1).astype(float)         # (N,)
    opp_nb = adj @ (owner == -1).astype(float)       # (N,)
    opp_nonhome = (owner == -1)
    opp_nonhome[homes[1]] = False
    flips = (A > 0) & opp_nonhome[None, :] & (my_nb[None, :] + A >= opp_nb[None, :])  # (k, N)
    frontier = adj @ (pts * (owner == 0).astype(float))  # (N,)
    # Contestedness of each flipped cell: how close the neighbour balance is to a tie.
    # A cell that flips by a wide margin is a weak springboard; one that flips narrowly
    # was a live launch point, so denying it matters more. Smooth, in (0, 1].
    margin = (my_nb + A) - opp_nb                    # (k, N), >= 0 where flips
    contest = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.abs(margin))           # (k, N)
    weight = flips.astype(float) * contest
    return (weight @ frontier) / tot
```

This computes the experiment's frontier-denial sum but weights each flipped opponent cell by `1/(1+|neighbour margin|)`, so narrowly-flipped (live springboard) cells count more than lopsided ones — a smooth reweighting that orders candidates differently from `flip_cascade_gain`; I read the "orders candidates differently" instruction as licensing this contestedness factor while keeping the frontier (empty-cell points) as the core quantity.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Immediate claim+flip point gain minus the opponent's best immediate claim+flip reply, normalised by total points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    k = moves.shape[0]
    N = owner.shape[0]

    A = adj[moves]                                   # (k,N)
    my_nb = adj @ (owner == 1).astype(float)         # (N,)
    opp_nb = adj @ (owner == -1).astype(float)       # (N,)

    opp_nonhome = (owner == -1).copy()
    opp_nonhome[homes[1]] = False

    flips = (A > 0) & opp_nonhome[None, :] & (my_nb[None, :] + A >= opp_nb[None, :])  # (k,N)
    my_gain = pts[moves] + flips.astype(float) @ pts  # (k,)

    # Post-claim boards
    new_my = np.tile((owner == 1)[None, :], (k, 1))
    new_my[np.arange(k), moves] = True
    new_my |= flips
    new_opp = np.tile((owner == -1)[None, :], (k, 1)) & ~flips

    my_cnt = new_my.astype(float) @ adj               # (k,N)
    opp_cnt = new_opp.astype(float) @ adj             # (k,N)

    # Opponent legal replies: empty cells adjacent to opponent cells, excluding the just-claimed cell
    legal = ((new_opp.astype(float) @ adj) > 0) & (owner == 0)[None, :]
    legal[np.arange(k), moves] = False

    my_nonhome = (owner == 1).copy()
    my_nonhome[homes[0]] = False

    # cond[i,e,d]: opponent claiming e flips my cell d
    cond = (opp_cnt[:, None, :] + adj[None, :, :] >= my_cnt[:, None, :]) & my_nonhome[None, None, :]
    reply = pts[None, :] + np.einsum('ied,d->ie', cond.astype(float), pts)  # (k,N)
    reply = np.where(legal, reply, 0.0)
    best_reply = reply.max(axis=1)                    # (k,)

    return (my_gain - best_reply) / tot

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Points of empty cells adjacent to opponent non-home cells this claim would flip, weighted by how contested each flipped cell is (own vs opponent neighbour balance), normalised by total board points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    A = adj[moves]                                   # (k, N)
    my_nb = adj @ (owner == 1).astype(float)         # (N,)
    opp_nb = adj @ (owner == -1).astype(float)       # (N,)
    opp_nonhome = (owner == -1)
    opp_nonhome[homes[1]] = False
    flips = (A > 0) & opp_nonhome[None, :] & (my_nb[None, :] + A >= opp_nb[None, :])  # (k, N)
    frontier = adj @ (pts * (owner == 0).astype(float))  # (N,)
    # Contestedness of each flipped cell: how close the neighbour balance is to a tie.
    # A cell that flips by a wide margin is a weak springboard; one that flips narrowly
    # was a live launch point, so denying it matters more. Smooth, in (0, 1].
    margin = (my_nb + A) - opp_nb                    # (k, N), >= 0 where flips
    contest = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.abs(margin))           # (k, N)
    weight = flips.astype(float) * contest
    return (weight @ frontier) / tot

Weighting each flipped cell by the points of the *empty* cells adjacent to it (and not by its own points or margin) makes the feature rank candidates by denied access rather than by flip likelihood, so it is complementary to f001 rather than a copy.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Points of empty cells I reach strictly sooner than the opponent after claiming each candidate, normalised by total points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    INF = 1e6
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    emp = (owner == 0)

    def bfs(sources, allowed):
        d = np.full(N, INF, dtype=float)
        d[sources] = 0.0
        for step in range(1, N + 1):
            frontier = (d == step - 1)
            if not frontier.any():
                break
            nb = frontier.astype(float) @ adj
            new = (nb > 0) & (d > step) & allowed
            if not new.any():
                break
            d[new] = step
        return d

    d_me = bfs(my, emp | my)
    d_op = bfs(opp, emp | opp)

    k = moves.shape[0]
    d_m = np.full((k, N), INF, dtype=float)
    d_m[np.arange(k), moves] = 0.0
    for step in range(1, N + 1):
        frontier = (d_m == step - 1)
        if not frontier.any():
            break
        nb = frontier.astype(float) @ adj
        new = (nb > 0) & (d_m > step) & emp[None, :]
        if not new.any():
            break
        d_m[new] = step

    d_new = np.minimum(d_me[None, :], d_m)
    margin = d_op[None, :] - d_new
    weight = (margin > 0).astype(float) + 0.5 * (margin == 0).astype(float)
    val = pts[None, :] * weight * emp[None, :]
    return val.sum(axis=1) / tot

The champion has no feature that compares my distance to the opponent's; the neighbour margin only counts adjacent cells. Scoring a candidate by the points of empty cells it lets me reach strictly sooner than the opponent (graph distance through claimable cells) directly measures that race.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Point value of the claimed cell, gated by how late the game is: early game values only defensible/connected cells, late game values raw points; zeros when irrelevant."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    theirs = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    my_nb = adjacency @ mine
    op_nb = adjacency @ theirs
    # how contested the candidate is: more of my support -> safer
    margin = my_nb[moves] - op_nb[moves]
    support = my_nb[moves] + 1.0
    safety = margin / (support + 1.0)          # in ~[-1, 1]
    val = points[moves].astype(float) / 5.0
    # game phase: 0 early (turn small) -> 1 late (board nearly full)
    total_claims = max(N - 2, 1)
    phase = min(max(turn / total_claims, 0.0), 1.0)
    # early: value only safe high-point cells; late: value raw points
    early = np.clip(safety, 0.0, 1.0) * val
    late = val
    out = (1.0 - phase) * early + phase * late
    return out
feature.measures: Point value of the claimed cell, gated by how late the game is: early game values only defensible/connected cells, late game values raw points; zeros when irrelevant.

feature.name: neighborhood_safety_context
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Neighbour margin of each candidate measured on the cells *around* it (second ring, excluding itself): sum over neighbours v of (my_nb(v) - op_nb(v))/(my_nb(v)+op_nb(v)+1), weighted by v's points and by whether v is still empty/contested, scaled by candidate value."""
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    theirs = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    my_nb = adjacency @ mine          # (N,) my-owned neighbours per cell
    op_nb = adjacency @ theirs        # (N,) opp-owned neighbours per cell
    local = (my_nb - op_nb) / (my_nb + op_nb + 1.0)   # safety of each cell
    # weight neighbour cells by their value and by how contested/valuable they are to grab next
    contested = (owner == 0).astype(float)            # empty cells still up for grabs
    w = (points.astype(float) / 5.0) * (0.5 + 0.5 * contested)
    # second-ring context: sum of local safety over neighbours of each candidate
    adj_f = adjacency.astype(float)
    ring = adj_f @ (local * w)                        # (N,) context around each cell
    # normalise by degree so high-degree cells aren't just bigger
    deg = adj_f.sum(axis=1)
    ring = ring / (deg + 1.0)
    # also include the candidate's own safety lightly (thread kept from parent)
    own = local[moves] * (points[moves] / 5.0)
    return 0.5 * own + ring[moves]

import numpy as np
import math

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: the points-weighted count of my own vulnerable non-home cells it would shield, minus the points-weighted count of my existing cells it would expose to flipping by the opponent, measured from the resulting neighbour-margin change (defensive consolidation value)."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    theirs = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    my_nb = adj @ mine
    op_nb = adj @ theirs
    # margin of each cell: positive = I dominate it (safe from opponent flip / ready to flip)
    margin = my_nb - op_nb
    # candidate contributes +1 to my_nb of its neighbours, raising their margin by adjacency
    adj_m = adj[moves]                       # (k, N)
    margin_after = margin[None, :] + adj_m   # (k, N)
    delta = margin_after - margin[None, :]   # (k, N) = adj_m, positive shifts only
    is_my_cell = (owner == 1)[None, :]
    allow = np.ones(N, bool)
    allow[homes[0]] = False
    allow = allow[None, :]
    # For my non-home cells: a claim that pushes margin from negative/low to >=0 protects them.
    was_vulnerable = (margin[None, :] < 0) & is_my_cell & allow
    now_safe = (margin_after >= 0) & was_vulnerable
    protect = (now_safe * points[None, :]).sum(axis=1)
    # For opponent cells: a claim that makes margin >= 0 sets up a flip next turn (soft pressure).
    is_op = (owner == -1)[None, :]
    op_allow = np.ones(N, bool)
    op_allow[homes[1]] = False
    op_allow = op_allow[None, :]
    pressure = (((margin_after >= 0) & is_op & op_allow) * points[None, :]).sum(axis=1)
    total = max(points.sum(), 1.0)
    return (protect + 0.5 * pressure) / total

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Frontier growth: number of empty cells adjacent to the candidate (after claiming it), scaled by point value, minus a term for empty cells the opponent could grab next turn."""
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    theirs = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    empty = (owner == 0).astype(float)
    opp_home = homes[1]
    my_home = homes[0]

    # empty neighbours of each candidate would be newly reachable by me
    adj_m = adjacency[moves]                       # (k, N)
    new_empty_mine = adj_m @ empty                 # (k,)

    # empty cells already adjacent to opponent (they can grab them) - penalise expanding there
    opp_reach = (adjacency @ theirs)                # (N,) count-ish, but binary-ish matter
    opp_front = ((opp_reach > 0) & (owner == 0)).astype(float)
    contestable = adj_m @ opp_front                # (k,)

    val = points[moves] / 5.0
    return val * (new_empty_mine - 0.7 * contestable) / 8.0

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Score of the flip cascade a claim could trigger: opponent cells adjacent to the claim weighted by their points, minus own cells that would be outnumbered and lost."""
    N = len(owner)
    my_count = (owner == 1).astype(int)
    opp_count = (owner == -1).astype(int)
    adj = adjacency.astype(int)
    # after claiming each candidate, my neighbour count on that cell's neighbours
    # candidate claim: add 1 to my_count at that cell
    # for each candidate m, compute hypothetical my neighbour counts of opponent cells adjacent to m
    k = len(moves)
    out = np.zeros(k)
    total_points = float(points.sum()) or 1.0
    own_home = homes[0]
    opp_home = homes[1]
    for i, m in enumerate(moves):
        # neighbours of m
        nb = np.where(adjacency[m])[0]
        gain = 0.0
        for c in nb:
            if c == opp_home or owner[c] != -1:
                continue
            # after claim, my neighbour count of c includes m as owned
            nbrs_c = np.where(adjacency[c])[0]
            my_n = my_count[nbrs_c].sum() + (1 if m not in nbrs_c else 0)  # m is a neighbour of c
            # m is neighbour of c, and m becomes owned -> my_count already counts owners; add 1
            my_n = my_count[nbrs_c].sum()
            if m in nbrs_c:
                my_n += 1
            opp_n = opp_count[nbrs_c].sum()
            if my_n >= opp_n:
                gain += points[c]
        out[i] = gain
    # normalise
    return out / total_points
feature.measures: Score of the flip cascade a claim could trigger: opponent cells adjacent to the claim weighted by their points, minus own cells that would be outnumbered and lost.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Net point swing of the immediate claim+flip: points gained by me minus points the opponent loses, per candidate, normalised."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    # neighbours counts for each cell
    # For each candidate c: after claiming c, my ownership gains 1 at c.
    # A neighbour v of c owned by opponent flips if my_neighbours(v) >= opp_neighbours(v) after claim,
    # and v is not opponent's home.
    adj = adjacency.astype(np.int32)
    my_count = adj @ my.astype(np.int32)      # (N,) my neighbours per cell
    opp_count = adj @ opp.astype(np.int32)    # (N,) opp neighbours per cell
    # after claiming candidate c, my_count at neighbour v increases by 1 if adj[v,c]
    cand = moves
    # my_count_after[v, c] = my_count[v] + adj[v,c]
    # flip condition at v given candidate c: v opponent, v != opp home, and my_count[v]+adj[v,c] >= opp_count[v]
    opp_home = homes[1]
    is_opp_cell = opp & (np.arange(N) != opp_home)
    # build (N, k)
    adj_c = adj[:, cand].astype(np.int32)             # (N, k)
    my_after = my_count[:, None] + adj_c              # (N, k)
    flips = is_opp_cell[:, None] & (my_after >= opp_count[:, None]) & (adj_c > 0)
    flip_pts = (flips * points[:, None]).sum(axis=0)  # (k,)
    claim_pts = points[cand].astype(float)
    total_pts = float(points.sum()) + 1e-9
    return (claim_pts + flip_pts) / total_pts
feature.measures: Net point swing of the immediate claim+flip: points gained by me minus points the opponent loses, per candidate, normalised.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Point value of the claimed cell, gated by how late the game is: early game values only defensible/connected cells, late game values raw points; zeros when irrelevant."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    theirs = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    my_nb = adjacency @ mine
    op_nb = adjacency @ theirs
    # how contested the candidate is: more of my support -> safer
    margin = my_nb[moves] - op_nb[moves]
    support = my_nb[moves] + 1.0
    safety = margin / (support + 1.0)          # in ~[-1, 1]
    val = points[moves].astype(float) / 5.0
    # game phase: 0 early (turn small) -> 1 late (board nearly full)
    total_claims = max(N - 2, 1)
    phase = min(max(turn / total_claims, 0.0), 1.0)
    # early: value only safe high-point cells; late: value raw points
    early = np.clip(safety, 0.0, 1.0) * val
    late = val
    out = (1.0 - phase) * early + phase * late
    return out
feature.measures: Point value of the claimed cell, gated by how late the game is: early game values only defensible/connected cells, late game values raw points; zeros when irrelevant.

feature.name: neighborhood_safety_context
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Neighbour margin of each candidate measured on the cells *around* it (second ring, excluding itself): sum over neighbours v of (my_nb(v) - op_nb(v))/(my_nb(v)+op_nb(v)+1), weighted by v's points and by whether v is still empty/contested, scaled by candidate value."""
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    theirs = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    my_nb = adjacency @ mine          # (N,) my-owned neighbours per cell
    op_nb = adjacency @ theirs        # (N,) opp-owned neighbours per cell
    local = (my_nb - op_nb) / (my_nb + op_nb + 1.0)   # safety of each cell
    # weight neighbour cells by their value and by how contested/valuable they are to grab next
    contested = (owner == 0).astype(float)            # empty cells still up for grabs
    w = (points.astype(float) / 5.0) * (0.5 + 0.5 * contested)
    # second-ring context: sum of local safety over neighbours of each candidate
    adj_f = adjacency.astype(float)
    ring = adj_f @ (local * w)                        # (N,) context around each cell
    # normalise by degree so high-degree cells aren't just bigger
    deg = adj_f.sum(axis=1)
    ring = ring / (deg + 1.0)
    # also include the candidate's own safety lightly (thread kept from parent)
    own = local[moves] * (points[moves] / 5.0)
    return 0.5 * own + ring[moves]
feature.measures: Neighbour margin of each candidate measured on the cells *around* it (second ring, excluding itself): sum over neighbours v of (my_nb(v) - op_nb(v))/(my_nb(v)+op_nb(v)+1), weighted by v's points and by whether v is still empty/contested, scaled by candidate value.

feature.code:
import numpy as np
import math

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: the points-weighted count of my own vulnerable non-home cells it would shield, minus the points-weighted count of my existing cells it would expose to flipping by the opponent, measured from the resulting neighbour-margin change (defensive consolidation value)."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    theirs = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    my_nb = adj @ mine
    op_nb = adj @ theirs
    # margin of each cell: positive = I dominate it (safe from opponent flip / ready to flip)
    margin = my_nb - op_nb
    # candidate contributes +1 to my_nb of its neighbours, raising their margin by adjacency
    adj_m = adj[moves]                       # (k, N)
    margin_after = margin[None, :] + adj_m   # (k, N)
    delta = margin_after - margin[None, :]   # (k, N) = adj_m, positive shifts only
    is_my_cell = (owner == 1)[None, :]
    allow = np.ones(N, bool)
    allow[homes[0]] = False
    allow = allow[None, :]
    # For my non-home cells: a claim that pushes margin from negative/low to >=0 protects them.
    was_vulnerable = (margin[None, :] < 0) & is_my_cell & allow
    now_safe = (margin_after >= 0) & was_vulnerable
    protect = (now_safe * points[None, :]).sum(axis=1)
    # For opponent cells: a claim that makes margin >= 0 sets up a flip next turn (soft pressure).
    is_op = (owner == -1)[None, :]
    op_allow = np.ones(N, bool)
    op_allow[homes[1]] = False
    op_allow = op_allow[None, :]
    pressure = (((margin_after >= 0) & is_op & op_allow) * points[None, :]).sum(axis=1)
    total = max(points.sum(), 1.0)
    return (protect + 0.5 * pressure) / total

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Frontier growth: number of empty cells adjacent to the candidate (after claiming it), scaled by point value, minus a term for empty cells the opponent could grab next turn."""
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    theirs = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    empty = (owner == 0).astype(float)
    opp_home = homes[1]
    my_home = homes[0]

    # empty neighbours of each candidate would be newly reachable by me
    adj_m = adjacency[moves]                       # (k, N)
    new_empty_mine = adj_m @ empty                 # (k,)

    # empty cells already adjacent to opponent (they can grab them) - penalise expanding there
    opp_reach = (adjacency @ theirs)                # (N,) count-ish, but binary-ish matter
    opp_front = ((opp_reach > 0) & (owner == 0)).astype(float)
    contestable = adj_m @ opp_front                # (k,)

    val = points[moves] / 5.0
    return val * (new_empty_mine - 0.7 * contestable) / 8.0
feature.measures: Frontier growth: number of empty cells adjacent to the candidate (after claiming it), scaled by point value, minus a term for empty cells the opponent could grab next turn.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Immediate claim+flip point gain minus the opponent's best immediate claim+flip reply, normalised by total points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    k = moves.shape[0]
    N = owner.shape[0]

    A = adj[moves]                                   # (k,N)
    my_nb = adj @ (owner == 1).astype(float)         # (N,)
    opp_nb = adj @ (owner == -1).astype(float)       # (N,)

    opp_nonhome = (owner == -1).copy()
    opp_nonhome[homes[1]] = False

    flips = (A > 0) & opp_nonhome[None, :] & (my_nb[None, :] + A >= opp_nb[None, :])  # (k,N)
    my_gain = pts[moves] + flips.astype(float) @ pts  # (k,)

    # Post-claim boards
    new_my = np.tile((owner == 1)[None, :], (k, 1))
    new_my[np.arange(k), moves] = True
    new_my |= flips
    new_opp = np.tile((owner == -1)[None, :], (k, 1)) & ~flips

    my_cnt = new_my.astype(float) @ adj               # (k,N)
    opp_cnt = new_opp.astype(float) @ adj             # (k,N)

    # Opponent legal replies: empty cells adjacent to opponent cells, excluding the just-claimed cell
    legal = ((new_opp.astype(float) @ adj) > 0) & (owner == 0)[None, :]
    legal[np.arange(k), moves] = False

    my_nonhome = (owner == 1).copy()
    my_nonhome[homes[0]] = False

    # cond[i,e,d]: opponent claiming e flips my cell d
    cond = (opp_cnt[:, None, :] + adj[None, :, :] >= my_cnt[:, None, :]) & my_nonhome[None, None, :]
    reply = pts[None, :] + np.einsum('ied,d->ie', cond.astype(float), pts)  # (k,N)
    reply = np.where(legal, reply, 0.0)
    best_reply = reply.max(axis=1)                    # (k,)

    return (my_gain - best_reply) / tot

The games we lose are those where the cell we take hands the opponent a bigger claim+flip straight back. Scoring my immediate swing minus the opponent's best immediate reply should therefore cut exactly the exchanges that cost us points, and it must be measured against the *actual best reply*, not a static count.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Points of empty cells adjacent to opponent non-home cells this claim would flip, weighted by how contested each flipped cell is (own vs opponent neighbour balance), normalised by total board points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    A = adj[moves]                                   # (k, N)
    my_nb = adj @ (owner == 1).astype(float)         # (N,)
    opp_nb = adj @ (owner == -1).astype(float)       # (N,)
    opp_nonhome = (owner == -1)
    opp_nonhome[homes[1]] = False
    flips = (A > 0) & opp_nonhome[None, :] & (my_nb[None, :] + A >= opp_nb[None, :])  # (k, N)
    frontier = adj @ (pts * (owner == 0).astype(float))  # (N,)
    # Contestedness of each flipped cell: how close the neighbour balance is to a tie.
    # A cell that flips by a wide margin is a weak springboard; one that flips narrowly
    # was a live launch point, so denying it matters more. Smooth, in (0, 1].
    margin = (my_nb + A) - opp_nb                    # (k, N), >= 0 where flips
    contest = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.abs(margin))           # (k, N)
    weight = flips.astype(float) * contest
    return (weight @ frontier) / tot

idea.hypothesis: f001, f003 and f006 are one idea (|rho|>=0.9) because they all weight a flip by how close it is to succeeding. That is a re-expression, not a new measurement. A flip is worth something different: it deletes an opponent cell that was that player's springboard to the empty cells it can still claim. Weighting each flipped cell by the points of the *empty* cells adjacent to it (and not by its own points or margin) makes the feature rank candidates by denied access rather than by flip likelihood, so it is complementary to f001 rather than a copy.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Points of empty cells I reach strictly sooner than the opponent after claiming each candidate, normalised by total points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    INF = 1e6
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    emp = (owner == 0)

    def bfs(sources, allowed):
        d = np.full(N, INF, dtype=float)
        d[sources] = 0.0
        for step in range(1, N + 1):
            frontier = (d == step - 1)
            if not frontier.any():
                break
            nb = frontier.astype(float) @ adj
            new = (nb > 0) & (d > step) & allowed
            if not new.any():
                break
            d[new] = step
        return d

    d_me = bfs(my, emp | my)
    d_op = bfs(opp, emp | opp)

    k = moves.shape[0]
    d_m = np.full((k, N), INF, dtype=float)
    d_m[np.arange(k), moves] = 0.0
    for step in range(1, N + 1):
        frontier = (d_m == step - 1)
        if not frontier.any():
            break
        nb = frontier.astype(float) @ adj
        new = (nb > 0) & (d_m > step) & emp[None, :]
        if not new.any():
            break
        d_m[new] = step

    d_new = np.minimum(d_me[None, :], d_m)
    margin = d_op[None, :] - d_new
    weight = (margin > 0).astype(float) + 0.5 * (margin == 0).astype(float)
    val = pts[None, :] * weight * emp[None, :]
    return val.sum(axis=1) / tot

The champion has no feature that compares my distance to the opponent's; the neighbour margin only counts adjacent cells. Scoring a candidate by the points of empty cells it lets me reach strictly sooner than the opponent (graph distance through claimable cells) directly measures that race.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """At-risk points removed: points of my non-home cells that stop being one opponent claim away from being outnumbered, normalised by total points."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    tot = points.sum() + 1.0
    adj = adjacency.astype(float)
    my_nb = adj @ (owner == 1).astype(float)
    opp_nb = adj @ (owner == -1).astype(float)
    legal_opp = (owner == 0) & ((adj @ (owner == -1).astype(float)) > 0)
    threat = adj @ legal_opp.astype(float)
    my_nonhome = (owner == 1)
    my_nonhome[homes[0]] = False
    risk_now = my_nonhome & (my_nb <= opp_nb + 1) & (threat > 0)
    A = adj[moves]  # (k, N)
    my_nb_new = my_nb[None, :] + A
    threat_new = threat[None, :] - A * legal_opp[moves][:, None].astype(float)
    risk_new = my_nonhome[None, :] & (my_nb_new <= opp_nb[None, :] + 1) & (threat_new > 0)
    removed = (risk_now[None, :] & ~risk_new).astype(float)
    return (removed @ pts) / tot

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],

```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `moves`: shape (k,), int: the cells you may claim (the candidates), in random order. Index into the per-cell arrays below.
- `owner`: shape (N,), int8: for every cell on the board: 1 = yours, -1 = the opponent's, 0 = empty (N = number of cells).
- `homes`: shape (2,), int: your home cell and the opponent's home cell (homes never flip).
- `points`: shape (N,), int: what each cell is worth (1, 2 or 5).
- `adjacency`: shape (N, N), bool: which cells are neighbours (symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `turn`: int: how many claims (by both players) have been made so far in this game; the game lasts N - 2 claims.
- Your current score is `points[owner == 1].sum()`, the opponent's `points[owner == -1].sum()`.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)). The highest-scoring candidate is claimed.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest).
